subject: math
cluster: Draw, construct, and describe geometrical figures and describe the relationships between them
skillName: Drawing Geometric Shapes with Given Conditions
intro: Test sets of conditions to decide whether they can build a triangle and, if so, whether the triangle is unique. Use the triangle inequality for sides, the $180^\circ$ angle-sum rule for angles, and the congruence criteria SSS, SAS, ASA, and AAS for uniqueness. Remember that AAA fixes shape but not size, and that SSA can be ambiguous.

items.prompt: Can a triangle be drawn with side lengths $3\text{ cm}$, $4\text{ cm}$, and $5\text{ cm}$? Answer yes or no and explain.

steps: Check the triangle inequality: the sum of the two shorter sides must exceed the longest side.
The two shorter sides are $3$ and $4$, and the longest is $5$.
Compute $3 + 4 = 7$, and $7 > 5$.
Since the two shorter sides sum to more than the longest side, a triangle can be drawn.

items.prompt: Can a triangle be drawn with side lengths $2\text{ cm}$, $3\text{ cm}$, and $9\text{ cm}$? Answer yes or no and explain.

steps: Apply the triangle inequality using the two shorter sides $2$ and $3$ against the longest side $9$.
Compute $2 + 3 = 5$.
Compare: $5 < 9$, so the two shorter sides do not reach across the longest side.
No triangle can be drawn.

items.prompt: Can a triangle have interior angles measuring $60^\circ$, $60^\circ$, and $60^\circ$? Answer yes or no and explain.

steps: The three interior angles of a triangle must sum to exactly $180^\circ$.
Add the angles: $60 + 60 + 60 = 180$.
The sum equals $180^\circ$, so these angles can form a triangle (an equilateral triangle).

items.prompt: Can a triangle have interior angles measuring $50^\circ$, $60^\circ$, and $90^\circ$? Answer yes or no and explain.

steps: Check whether the three angles sum to $180^\circ$.
Add the angles: $50 + 60 + 90 = 200$.
Since $200^\circ \ne 180^\circ$, these angles cannot form a triangle.

items.prompt: Can a triangle be drawn with side lengths $6\text{ cm}$, $6\text{ cm}$, and $6\text{ cm}$? Answer yes or no and name the type of triangle.

steps: Apply the triangle inequality: $6 + 6 = 12 > 6$, so a triangle can be drawn.
All three sides are equal in length.
A triangle with three equal sides is called an equilateral triangle.
solution.answer: Yes; it is an equilateral triangle because all three sides are $6\text{ cm}$.

items.prompt: A triangle is given by two sides of $6\text{ cm}$ and $8\text{ cm}$ with an included angle of $40^\circ$ between them. Does this determine a unique triangle? Name the congruence criterion.

steps: Two sides are given along with the angle located between them (the included angle).
This matches the Side-Angle-Side pattern.
SAS fixes the lengths of the two sides and the opening between them, so the third side and remaining angles are forced.
Therefore exactly one triangle (up to congruence) can be drawn.

items.prompt: A triangle has a base of $7\text{ cm}$ with a $45^\circ$ angle at one end of the base and a $60^\circ$ angle at the other end. Does this determine a unique triangle? Name the congruence criterion.

steps: A side (the $7\text{ cm}$ base) is given with the two angles at its endpoints.
This is the Angle-Side-Angle pattern, with the side included between the two angles.
ASA fixes the base length and the two directions the other sides travel, so their intersection point is determined.
Exactly one triangle can be drawn.

items.prompt: The conditions are three angles measuring $50^\circ$, $60^\circ$, and $70^\circ$ with no side length given. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Explain.

steps: First check feasibility: $50 + 60 + 70 = 180$, so the angles are valid.
Only the three angles are fixed (AAA); no side length is specified.
Angles determine the shape of the triangle but not its size.
You can scale the triangle to any size and still keep these angles, so infinitely many similar triangles satisfy the conditions.
solution.answer: More than one triangle (infinitely many similar triangles), because AAA fixes the shape but not the size.

items.prompt: Can a triangle be drawn with side lengths $3\text{ cm}$, $4\text{ cm}$, and $7\text{ cm}$? Answer yes or no and explain what figure results.

steps: Apply the triangle inequality to the two shorter sides $3$ and $4$ against the longest side $7$.
Compute $3 + 4 = 7$.
Since $3 + 4 = 7$ exactly equals the longest side, the two shorter sides lie flat along the longest side.
The figure collapses into a straight segment, so no triangle is formed (this is a degenerate case).
solution.answer: No; since $3 + 4 = 7$, the sides form a straight segment, not a triangle.

items.prompt: Using a ruler and protractor, you must construct a triangle with a $5\text{ cm}$ side, a $5\text{ cm}$ side, and a $40^\circ$ angle included between those two sides. Describe the construction steps and state whether the triangle is unique.

steps: Draw one $5\text{ cm}$ segment with the ruler; label its endpoints $A$ and $B$.
At endpoint $A$, use the protractor to measure a $40^\circ$ angle from segment $AB$.
Along that new ray, mark off $5\text{ cm}$ with the ruler and label the point $C$.
Connect $B$ to $C$ to close the triangle.
Two sides and their included angle are fixed, which is the SAS condition, so the triangle is unique.
solution.answer: The construction gives a unique triangle, by SAS.

items.prompt: A triangle has two known angles of $35^\circ$ and $85^\circ$ and one known side of $10\text{ cm}$ that lies between them. Find the third angle, then state whether the triangle is unique and name the criterion.

steps: Use the angle-sum rule: the three angles total $180^\circ$.
Subtract the known angles: $180 - 35 - 85 = 60$, so the third angle is $60^\circ$.
The given $10\text{ cm}$ side lies between the $35^\circ$ and $85^\circ$ angles, which is the Angle-Side-Angle pattern.
ASA determines a unique triangle.
solution.answer: The third angle is $60^\circ$, and the triangle is unique by ASA.

items.prompt: Two sides of a triangle measure $5\text{ cm}$ and $9\text{ cm}$. Find the range of possible lengths $x$ for the third side so that a triangle can be formed.

steps: For any triangle, the third side $x$ must satisfy $|a - b| < x < a + b$.
Here $a = 5$ and $b = 9$.
Compute the lower bound: $|5 - 9| = 4$.
Compute the upper bound: $5 + 9 = 14$.
So the third side must satisfy $4 < x < 14$.

items.prompt: Sides $a = 5\text{ cm}$ and $b = 8\text{ cm}$ are given, along with a non-included angle $A = 30^\circ$ that lies opposite side $a$. The height from the given angle to the line of side $b$ is $h = b\sin A = 8 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 4\text{ cm}$. Using the comparison of $a$ to $h$ and to $b$, determine how many triangles can be formed.

steps: This is the ambiguous SSA case (two sides and a non-included angle), so count carefully.
Compute the reference height: $h = b\sin A = 8 \cdot \sin 30^\circ = 8 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 4\text{ cm}$.
Compare the side opposite the angle, $a = 5$, with $h = 4$ and with $b = 8$.
Since $h < a < b$, that is $4 < 5 < 8$, the side $a$ is long enough to reach the base in two distinct positions.
Therefore two non-congruent triangles satisfy these conditions.
solution.answer: Two triangles, because $h = 4 < a = 5 < b = 8$ is the two-solution SSA case.

items.prompt: A student claims that knowing all three angles of a triangle is enough to draw exactly one triangle. Explain why this claim is false, and state one additional piece of information that would make the triangle unique.
items.answer: False; AAA gives infinitely many similar triangles. Adding any one side length makes it unique.

steps: Three angles (AAA) fix only the shape of the triangle, not its size.
Any triangle with the same three angles can be enlarged or shrunk and still match, giving infinitely many similar triangles.
So three angles alone do not determine a unique triangle; the claim is false.
Supplying any one side length pins down the size. For example, giving a side between two of the angles turns it into an ASA condition, which is unique.
solution.answer: False: AAA gives infinitely many similar triangles. Providing any one side length (for example via ASA or AAS) makes the triangle unique.

items.prompt: A triangle is to be built with a fixed side of $6\text{ cm}$, a $40^\circ$ angle at one end of that side, and a second side of length $x$ drawn from that same $40^\circ$ angle. Determine the relationship that side $x$ must have to the fixed side so the result is a single unique triangle, and name the criterion that applies once both side lengths and the included angle are set.
items.answer: Any positive $x$ gives a unique triangle by SAS

steps: The $40^\circ$ angle sits between the fixed $6\text{ cm}$ side and the side of length $x$, so it is the included angle.
Once you fix two side lengths and the angle between them, the third side and the other two angles are completely determined.
This is the Side-Angle-Side (SAS) condition, which always yields a unique triangle.
So any positive value of $x$ produces exactly one triangle; there is no ambiguity because the angle is included, not opposite a side.
solution.answer: For any positive $x$, the included $40^\circ$ angle makes this an SAS condition, so the triangle is unique.
